newsitem.title: USA: California flood victims sue state over levee break.
newsitem.headline: California flood victims sue state over levee break.

text.p: Six flood victims sued the state of California on Tuesday, alleging it had failed to maintain a levee that broke during recent winter storms, flooding hundreds of homes and a wide area of farmland.
The lawsuit, one of the first filed since the early January flooding, seeks unspecified damages for property losses and compensation for emotional distress.
Alice Wolfson, an attorney for the homeowners, said the goal of the suit was to compensate the victims and to force the state to make repairs to prevent future disasters.
California state emergency officials said they had no immediate comment.

The plaintiffs in the suit -- six Yuba County, Calif., residents -- alleged that the state knowingly refused to make repairs to prevent a levee along the Feather River from collapsing and flooding the towns of Arboga and Olivehurst.

The state knew the levee needed to be repaired, but ignored warnings by civil engineers and others as early as 1991 that the levee was prone to failure, according to the lawsuit, filed in Superior Court in Yuba County.

Lawyers for the flood victims said they were not seeking class action status at this time. The attorneys said, however, that they expected to file lawsuits on behalf of other victims and seek to consolidate the cases in the coming months.

A levee on the rain-swollen Feather River burst in early January, inundating homes and farmland about 50 miles (80 kms) northeast of Sacramento. The break was responsible for at least three deaths, according to the lawsuit. About 200 homes and businesses were destroyed, and over 500 buildings damaged.

The Feather River break was one of several in northern and central California during the New Year storms. Statewide, damage estimates from the floods have surpassed $1.5 billion. Nearly 16,000 homes have been damaged or destroyed.
Officials said the floods were almost certain to be the most costly in state history, overtaking the $1.8 billion of losses suffered in 1995 floods.
